findings.text: The first paragraph tells a newcomer what Athena is, who it is for and what problem it solves, before any study content. The what and the why are both covered.
findings.source: header lede: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository... It solves the problem of AI edits that arrive unreviewed and unaccountable."

findings.text: The page explains why a site named for Athena is mostly about another project, firstmate. That heads off the most likely confusion. Even so, almost the whole page is about firstmate, so a reader who came to learn about Athena gets only three header paragraphs and the Next steps section on it.
findings.source: header lede: "A study is Athena's written reading of another software project... Athena made this study of firstmate to show that it can read an unfamiliar project"

findings.text: The next step is concrete: prerequisites, a clone command, an install command and a first command, with what it does. The header also links straight here, so a newcomer does not need to scroll the study to find it.
findings.source: Next steps: "Get the code: git clone ...", "Install Athena from the checkout: ./setup.sh", "Try it with a one-line request: athena ask \"add a changelog\""

findings.text: The page says Athena is written in Rust, but the prerequisites list no Rust toolchain. It does not say whether setup.sh installs one, so a newcomer may not know whether they need cargo.
findings.source: Next steps: "have git 2.40 or later, a C linker, curl, and either Claude Code or npm"; lede: "written in Rust"

findings.text: The page's main promise is a traceable commit with cost and verdict, but nothing on the page shows one. The firstmate study shows claim-to-source tracing, not the request-to-commit flow the newcomer is asked to try.
findings.source: lede: "get back a commit they can trace to the request, the models, the cost and the verdict"

findings.text: This header link is meant for the project owner. A newcomer does not know who the owner is or what proposals are meant, so it is noise at the top of the page.
findings.source: header: "Owner view: proposals waiting for your decision."

findings.text: The Counters section refers to transitions by id before the Transitions section defines them, so a first-time reader meets t1, t3 and so on with no context.
findings.source: Counters: "places-held, changed by transitions t1, t3, t4, t9, t11"

findings.text: The definition uses the word "wake", which is never defined anywhere on the page, so the term is still unclear.
findings.source: Glossary, stale wake: "A wake after which the agent inspects a worker that may have stopped, looped or gone quiet."

findings.text: The firstmate study opens well. A short definition, then key words defined before use, then one task followed start to finish, all give a newcomer a way in before the dense state and transition cards.
findings.source: Start here, What firstmate is: "Firstmate is a tool for people who direct AI coding agents. It keeps a backlog of programming tasks and hands each one to a worker"

findings.text: Hedges like "the cited text states no..." come up again and again. They are honest, but they make the page read like an audit, and they slow a newcomer down.
findings.source: When things go wrong: "The cited text states no count or limit on retries of a failed backlog close... so a close is not replayed until a session starts."

findings.text: This section is about the inside of the repository and means nothing to a first-time visitor. Nothing is lost, but it adds nothing for this reader.
findings.source: About this page: "is the name of the folder under studies/ that holds the data this page is generated from."
